stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ostrow's conclusion?
stimulus: Marine biologist Rana Ostrow placed fragments of staghorn coral in two aquariums. The tanks received identical light, water, and nutrients, but only one also housed parrotfish, which graze on algae. After eight weeks, the coral in the parrotfish tank had grown noticeably more than the coral in the other tank. Ostrow concluded that the parrotfish helped the coral grow by keeping algae from covering and shading it.
choices: The coral fragments in the parrotfish tank grew larger over eight weeks than the coral fragments in the other tank did.
Algae covered far less of the coral's surface in the parrotfish tank than it covered in the tank without parrotfish.
Both tanks received the same amount of light each day during the full eight weeks that the experiment was running.
Parrotfish can be found grazing among the corals on most healthy reefs in tropical oceans around the world.
explanation: Ostrow's conclusion has two parts: the parrotfish reduced the algae, and less algae let the coral grow. The passage already tells you the coral grew more. The missing link is that the parrotfish tank had less algae on the coral. Choice B shows exactly that difference between the two tanks, so it supports the proposed mechanism.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You picked a choice that only repeats the observed result, which the passage already states. It says nothing about algae, so it gives no support for Ostrow's explanation of why the coral grew more.

C.why: This condition was the same for both tanks, and the passage already says so. A feature the two groups share can't explain why they turned out differently, so it doesn't support the algae explanation.

D.why: You were drawn by the topic of parrotfish on reefs. Where parrotfish live in the wild doesn't show that they reduced algae on the coral in this experiment.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?
stimulus: The human body cannot digest dietary fiber, but certain gut bacteria break it down and release butyrate, a compound that can reduce inflammation. In a twelve-week study, one group of adults ate a high-fiber diet while a second, otherwise similar group ate a low-fiber diet. By the end of the study, the high-fiber group had lower levels of inflammation markers in the blood. The researchers concluded that this difference arose because the high-fiber diet increased butyrate production.
choices: Adults in the high-fiber group had lower levels of inflammation markers in the blood than adults in the low-fiber group did.
Adults in the high-fiber group had higher levels of butyrate in the digestive tract than adults in the low-fiber group did.
Adults in both groups ate about the same number of calories each day during the twelve weeks that the study lasted.
Adults in the low-fiber group had higher levels of butyrate in the digestive tract than adults in the high-fiber group did.
explanation: The proposed chain runs from more fiber to more butyrate to less inflammation. The passage already reports less inflammation, so the claim depends on the middle link: the high-fiber group must have produced more butyrate. Choice B shows that difference, in the right direction.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You chose a restatement of the result the passage already reports. It doesn't mention butyrate, so it can't support the claim that butyrate caused the difference.

C.why: Calorie intake was the same for both groups, so it can't separate them. It also says nothing about butyrate, the mechanism the conclusion proposes.

D.why: You found the right comparison but missed its direction. If the low-fiber group made more butyrate, the researchers' explanation would be weakened, not supported.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the seismologists' conclusion?
stimulus: A moderate earthquake recently struck a region where a river valley lies next to a rocky ridge. Both areas are about 30 kilometers from the epicenter. Homes in the valley sit on loose river sediment, while homes on the ridge sit on solid bedrock. Although homes in the two areas are built in similar ways, the valley homes suffered far more cracking. A team of seismologists concluded that the valley's sediment amplified the ground shaking, which caused the greater damage.
choices: Homes in the valley showed much more cracking after the earthquake than homes on the nearby ridge showed.
Instruments in the valley recorded stronger ground shaking during the earthquake than instruments on the ridge did.
The valley and the ridge were each located about the same distance from the epicenter of the earthquake.
Earthquakes in the region have occurred beneath the valley more often than they have occurred beneath the ridge.
explanation: The seismologists claim the sediment made the shaking stronger and that stronger shaking caused more damage. The damage is already known. What still needs showing is that the shaking really was stronger in the valley than on the ridge. Choice B gives that measurement and separates the two areas.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You picked the observed result, the extra cracking, which the passage already states. It doesn't show that the shaking was stronger, so it adds no support for the amplification explanation.

C.why: The two areas share this distance, and the passage already says so. A feature common to both can't explain why they suffered different damage.

D.why: This concerns where earthquakes start over time, not how one earthquake's shaking differed between the two areas. Treating it as evidence of amplification goes beyond what the finding shows.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hydrologists' conclusion?
stimulus: Alder Creek and Birch Creek drain neighboring watersheds of nearly equal size and steepness. Three years ago, wetlands were restored along the upper reaches of Alder Creek, while the wetlands along Birch Creek remained drained. During a recent heavy storm, Birch Creek overflowed its banks, but Alder Creek did not. Hydrologists concluded that the restored wetlands held back much of the rainwater and released it slowly, keeping Alder Creek's flow below flood level.
choices: Birch Creek overflowed its banks during the heavy storm, while Alder Creek stayed within its banks the whole time.
The restored wetlands along Alder Creek filled with water during the storm and drained gradually over several days.
Both Alder Creek and Birch Creek usually carry more water in the spring than they carry in late summer each year.
Birch Creek's drained wetlands held back more of the storm's rainwater than Alder Creek's restored wetlands did.
explanation: The conclusion names a specific mechanism: the wetlands stored the rain and released it slowly. Choice B shows the restored wetlands doing exactly that during this storm, which links the restoration to the creek staying below flood level.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You chose a restatement of what happened, which the passage already reports. It doesn't show the wetlands storing and slowly releasing water, so it doesn't support the proposed cause.

C.why: This seasonal pattern is true of both creeks, so it can't explain why only Birch Creek flooded. It also doesn't involve the wetlands at all.

D.why: You reversed the comparison. If the drained wetlands held back more water, that would cut against the hydrologists' explanation rather than support it.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the engineers' conclusion?
stimulus: Engineers made two batches of a plastic that were identical except that one batch also contained tiny capsules filled with a liquid healing agent. They cracked samples from both batches and then let them rest for a day. When retested, the samples with capsules had regained most of their original strength, while the plain samples had not. The engineers concluded that the capsules broke open when the plastic cracked, releasing healing agent that filled and sealed the cracks.
choices: After resting for a day, the samples with capsules were much stronger when retested than the plain samples were.
Under a microscope, cracks in the samples with capsules were filled with hardened agent, while plain cracks were open.
Both batches of plastic were made from a material that manufacturers often use to build the bodies of drones.
Plastics containing capsules of healing agent can repair any crack, no matter how wide or long that crack is.
explanation: The engineers propose a mechanism: agent released from broken capsules filled the cracks. Choice B shows that mechanism in the capsule samples, where the cracks were filled with healing agent. It also shows that the cracks in the plain samples stayed open, so it accounts for the difference between the two batches.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You picked the observed result, the strength recovery, which the passage already describes. It doesn't show healing agent filling the cracks, so it adds no support for the proposed mechanism.

C.why: The base material is the same in both batches, so it can't explain why only one batch recovered. It's a side detail, not evidence about the capsules.

D.why: This claims far more than the experiment tested: any crack of any size. A sweeping claim like this doesn't show what happened inside these particular cracks.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Rehberg's hypothesis?
stimulus: At high altitude the air holds less oxygen, which can prompt the body to make more red blood cells, the cells that carry oxygen to working muscles. Sports scientist Tomasz Rehberg recruited 40 cyclists. For six weeks, half trained at a mountain camp and half trained at sea level, and both groups did identical workouts. Rehberg hypothesizes that the mountain group's red blood cell counts will increase but the sea-level group's will not.
choices: The red blood cell counts of cyclists in both groups rose by similar amounts over the six weeks of training.
The red blood cell counts of cyclists in the mountain group rose, while those in the sea-level group stayed about the same.
Cyclists in the mountain group said their workouts felt harder than cyclists in the sea-level group said theirs did.
The red blood cell counts of cyclists in the sea-level group rose, while those in the mountain group stayed about the same.
explanation: The hypothesis has two parts: the mountain group's counts go up, and the sea-level group's do not. Choice B confirms both, so it separates the two groups exactly as the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You picked a finding that is true of both groups equally. If both counts rose, the result does not separate mountain training from sea-level training, and the hypothesis says only one group's counts should rise.

C.why: You matched the topic, not the claim. How hard the workouts felt is not the red blood cell counts the hypothesis is about.

D.why: You reversed the groups. The hypothesis expects the mountain group's counts to rise, not the sea-level group's.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's conclusion?
stimulus: In a forest, soil and roots soak up much of the rain that falls. When the trees are cleared, more of that rain runs quickly over the ground into streams. Hydrologist Amara Lindqvist monitored two neighboring watersheds of similar size and slope through a season of storms. One was forested and the other had recently been logged. She concluded that logging speeds up runoff, so the logged watershed's stream peaks sooner after rain begins.
choices: Streamflow in the forested watershed peaked about two hours after rain began, compared with six hours in the logged watershed.
The logged watershed had much less tree cover and much more bare ground than the neighboring forested watershed had.
Streamflow in both watersheds rose sharply during each storm and then returned to normal levels within two days.
Streamflow in the logged watershed peaked about two hours after rain began, compared with six hours in the forested watershed.
explanation: The conclusion says the logged watershed's stream peaks sooner than the forested one's. Choice D shows the logged stream peaking four hours earlier, which is the difference between the two watersheds that the conclusion predicts.

A.why: You got the direction backward. Here the forested stream peaks first, which is the opposite of what the conclusion predicts.

B.why: You picked a choice that restates the setup. Saying the logged watershed has fewer trees tells you nothing about when either stream peaks, and timing is what the conclusion is about.

C.why: You picked a finding that is true of both watersheds equally. Because it applies to both streams in the same way, it can't show that the logged one peaks sooner.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Albarrán's hypothesis?
stimulus: Steel rusts much faster in salt water than in fresh water because dissolved salt speeds up the chemical reactions that form rust. Materials scientist Kenji Albarrán tested a new polymer coating by placing coated and uncoated steel plates in both kinds of water for 60 days. He hypothesizes that the coating greatly reduces rust in salt water but makes little difference in fresh water.
choices: In salt water, coated plates rusted far less than uncoated plates did; in fresh water, the two kinds rusted about equally.
In salt water and in fresh water alike, the coated plates rusted far less than the uncoated plates rusted.
Plates in salt water rusted far more than plates in fresh water did, whether or not they had been coated.
In fresh water, coated plates rusted far less than uncoated plates did; in salt water, the two kinds rusted about equally.
explanation: The hypothesis has two parts: the coating helps a lot in salt water, and it helps little in fresh water. Choice A confirms both parts.

B.why: You picked support for a broader claim. The hypothesis says the coating makes little difference in fresh water, but this choice has it working in both kinds of water.

C.why: You picked a choice that restates the background fact that salt water causes more rust. It holds for coated and uncoated plates alike, so it says nothing about what the coating does.

D.why: You swapped the two conditions. The hypothesis says the coating matters in salt water, not in fresh water.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nandakumar's hypothesis?
stimulus: Asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and release that stored heat slowly after sunset. Meteorologist Priya Nandakumar compared summer temperature readings from downtown weather stations with readings from stations on nearby farmland. She hypothesizes that the city's temperature advantage over the farmland is larger at night than during the day.
choices: The downtown stations stood on sites with more pavement and fewer trees than the farmland stations did.
Downtown stations averaged 4°C warmer than farmland stations at midday but only 1°C warmer at midnight.
Downtown stations averaged 1°C warmer than farmland stations at midday but fully 4°C warmer at midnight.
Downtown and farmland stations were both, on average, about 9°C cooler at midnight than at midday.
explanation: The hypothesis says the gap between city and farmland should be bigger at night. Choice C shows a 1°C gap at midday growing to 4°C at midnight, which is exactly that.

A.why: You picked a choice about the cause (pavement) rather than the predicted result. It doesn't show how the temperature gap changes between day and night.

B.why: You got the direction backward. In this choice the gap shrinks at night, but the hypothesis says it should grow.

D.why: You picked a finding that is true of both places equally. If both cooled by the same amount overnight, the gap would stay the same, so this does not support a larger gap at night.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Fonseca's hypothesis?
stimulus: On many reefs, fast-growing algae cover the hard surfaces where drifting coral larvae need to attach. Marine biologist Delia Fonseca set up two identical reef tanks with the same number of coral larvae and added algae-eating sea urchins to only one. She hypothesizes that the urchins, by eating algae, will leave more open surface, so more larvae will settle in that tank.
choices: The urchins grazed most actively at night and spent the daylight hours sheltering in narrow crevices in the tank.
The tank with urchins ended with less algae and more settled larvae than the tank without urchins did.
The tank with urchins ended with less algae than the other tank, but both had similar numbers of settled larvae.
The tank without urchins ended with less algae and more settled larvae than the tank with urchins did.
explanation: The hypothesis links a cause to an effect: urchins reduce algae, and less algae means more larvae settle. Choice B shows both links in the tank with urchins and neither in the other tank.

A.why: You matched the topic, not the claim. When the urchins feed is a side detail and says nothing about algae cover or larval settlement.

C.why: You stopped at the first part. This choice shows the urchins reduced algae, but it gives both tanks the same settlement, so the predicted effect on larvae never appears.

D.why: You reversed the tanks. The hypothesis predicts less algae and more larvae in the tank that has urchins, not in the one without them.
